title: Theyve Always Been This Way So Get Ready
author: The Daily Dad
summary: A short Daily Dad piece arguing that teenage attitude is not a personal affront but a developmental constant going back at least to ancient Greece. The frame comes from Emily Wilson's translation of Homer's Odyssey, where she lands on words like 'moodily,' 'brooding,' and 'sullen' to render the teenage Telemachus, and where in one scene Telemachus tries to speak out against the suitors and ends up bursting into tears. The piece treats this as evidence that curfew-blowing, door-slamming, and self-centred teenagers are an ancient tradition, not a modern parenting failure. The takeaway is preparatory rather than corrective: stop being surprised, stop taking it personally, prepare for it, and even appreciate it as the long human pattern. The piece is short by design — it lands on a single reframe — and is meant to lower the emotional temperature of parenting through the teen years rather than to provide a strategy.
points: Teenage moodiness, brooding, and self-centred behaviour show up in the Odyssey's portrait of Telemachus, which positions today's teen attitudes as ancient developmental patterns rather than modern parenting failures.
Wilson's translation lands on 'moodily,' 'brooding,' 'sullen,' and a scene where Telemachus bursts into tears mid-speech — a description that fits any contemporary teen.
The right parental response is preparatory: stop being surprised, don't take it personally, plan for it.
There is even an appreciative move available: this is a tradition, an ancient one, and it's somewhat reassuring that what seems like generational decline is actually generational continuity.
The piece is short by design and works as a single reframe to lower the emotional temperature of teen parenting, not as a strategy.
quotes: They blew past their curfew, again. They woke up grouchy, again. They ignored you and walked away in the middle of a conversation. They are convinced the world revolves around them. They think they know better about everything.

I have tried to make sure that a reader can feel inside the characters in the poem, to convey the ways that each character in the poem has her or his own distinctive point of view, the immaturity and vulnerability of Telemachus, for example, when he tries to speak out against the suitors, but ends up bursting into tears.

Some of the other words she translated for 'immature' Telemachus across the epic poem: Moodily. Brooding. Sullen. Sound familiar? That's every teenager ever. That was you. That is (or is going to be) your kid. That was every kid in ancient Greece, too.

Kids are kids. Always have been and always will be. Teenagers will do teenage things and have teenage attitudes. That's how it goes. It shouldn't surprise us. It shouldn't be taken personally, only prepared for.
If anything, it should be appreciated, because it's a tradition, apparently an ancient one, for them to be this way.” Archived from The Daily Dad on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
